name: Hard mewing

card.summary: Mewing with deliberate upward tongue pressure; discussed as a stronger version of tongue posture, with no research testing it and some users reporting masseter growth.
card.note: No published study has tested it; users report enlarged masseters and tooth gaps in combination with other practices.

quick.overview:
Hard mewing is a looksmaxxing term for pressing the tongue against the palate with deliberate force, as opposed to the light resting posture usually described as mewing. It is discussed on looksmax.org alongside chewing, thumb pulling, chin tucks and palate expansion.

Proponents report forward growth, a wider jaw and better breathing and posture. No published study has examined forceful tongue pressure as an appearance practice, and orthodontic bodies say mewing in general lacks evidence.
quick.mechanism: Believers say stronger and more sustained pressure from the tongue on the palate drives more bone remodelling than a relaxed resting posture, extending the orthotropic idea that tongue posture guides upper-jaw growth. Mechanical-loading research shows bone adapts to strain in general, but no study measures what tongue pressure does to the adult facial skeleton.
quick.risks: Users on forums report that hard mewing made their masseter muscles wider, changed how their cheeks looked and, in combination with thumb pulling and expanders, opened a gap between the front teeth. These are anecdotal reports. No clinical data exist on forceful tongue pressure.

lead: Hard mewing is a looksmaxxing term for a forceful version of mewing: pressing the whole tongue upward against the roof of the mouth with deliberate effort, rather than letting it rest there lightly.[3][6] The goal people state is a better-defined face, with a more forward upper jaw, a sharper jawline, hollower cheeks and a straighter head and neck posture, achieved without surgery.[8][21] Users treat it as the intensified stage of ordinary mewing and often pair it with chin tucks, chewing, thumb pulling and palate expansion.[10][20]

Mewing takes its name from British orthodontist John Mew (1928 to 2025), who developed orthotropics, a system that holds facial growth can be guided by tongue and lip posture and by wide dental arches, and from his son Mike Mew, who popularised the practice online.[2][15] Mew summarised the posture as standing up straight and shutting your mouth.[15] The term "hard mewing" is community vocabulary rather than an orthotropic term, and the posts that use it describe pressing harder and holding the position for long periods.[3][7][25]

No published study has tested hard mewing. Research on the wider orthotropic approach is limited to a 2007 twin study of professionally delivered treatment and commentary papers, and orthodontic bodies, including the American Association of Orthodontists, state there is no evidence mewing improves the jaw.[1][4][5]

paras: In forum usage, hard mewing means pushing the tongue firmly into the roof of the mouth, usually with the lips sealed and the teeth lightly together, in contrast to a relaxed resting posture.[3][21] Some users describe doing it continuously through the day and keeping a multi-year log of the habit.[24][26] One thread frames the distinction directly as "mewing vs hard mewing," with disagreement over whether the extra force adds anything.[3]

Orthotropic teaching, as summarised by Wikipedia, centres on a closed mouth, nasal breathing and a tongue resting against the palate, not on pressing hard.[15][5] Forum posters who promote hard mewing often justify it by saying more force produces more bone stimulation.[8][25]

John Mew, born in Royal Tunbridge Wells in 1928, qualified in dentistry in 1953 and later trained in orthognathic surgery. In 1958 he proposed the "Tropic Premise," the idea that malocclusion is a postural deformity largely driven by environment rather than genetics, which early intervention could prevent.[15] His orthotropic methods included palatal expanders, dietary changes and training the tongue to rest against the palate.[15] In a 1992 paper he proposed that tongue posture and a firm tongue-to-palate swallow influence oropharyngeal development and ear health, an idea he described as drawn from earlier hypotheses.[18]

The practice reached a large audience in 2019. Google Trends data shows interest in the term rising from January 2019, The Guardian covered it as a YouTube craze in March 2019, and the Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery published a commentary that year titled "Mewing: Social Media's Alternative to Orthognathic Surgery?"[5][4]

Within looksmaxxing forums the practice split into a gentle posture and a "hard" version, and hard mewing appears in threads including long-term progress journals and "why you should start hard mewing" posts.[24][25][26] A 2025 sociological analysis of 8,072 comments in a large looksmaxxing community described how members are encouraged to alter their bodies substantially, citing mewing as an example.[17]

Proponents say that tongue pressure on the palate acts as a natural palate expander, widening and advancing the maxilla, which in turn lifts the cheekbones, opens the airway and raises the lower jaw's position. Hard mewing extends that logic: more force or longer duration should mean more remodelling.[8][25] Some say it works best during growth and post results at ages 14 to 17, while others say it continues to help after puberty.[27][8]

Posters also say it fixes posture. One user credits hard mewing combined with chin tucks for improved neck-muscle stability and head position, while others report hollow cheeks or a more defined jawline.[8][9] A smaller strand claims benefits for breathing and, following Mew's own writing, for ear and airway health.[18]

Hard mewing is rarely done alone in the threads that describe it. One forum routine lists it with chewing gum, thumb pulling, belt pulling, bonesmashing and chin tucking as part of a daily regimen, and others combine it with maxillary expansion or a palatal expander.[10][20] Threads on the topic also ask whether a given user's overbite or recessed jaw changes how mewing should be done.[9]

Users disagree about its value. Some posters call hard mewing a decisive tool, one claiming it did more for them than hormones; others ask for photographic proof or title threads "stop hard mewing."[8][12][23] A thread asking what others think of hard mewing shows the same split.[23]

Wikipedia describes mewing as an unproven oral-posture practice, reports that no credible research has shown orthotropics works, and states that most orthodontists do not regard it as an alternative to orthognathic surgery.[5] The American Association of Orthodontists has said there is no evidence that mewing improves the jaw.[5]

The research that exists concerns orthotropic treatment by trained practitioners, not self-directed hard mewing. A 2007 study compared 12 sets of identical twins, one twin treated with traditional fixed appliances and the other with orthotropic growth-guidance treatment, and judged outcomes 10 years later using a panel of 12 lay judges, who rated most orthotropically treated twins as improved and most conventionally treated twins as less attractive; the authors reported little difference in dental results and more relapse in the conventional group.[1] A 2019 commentary examined mewing as a social-media alternative to jaw surgery, and a 2026 Journal of Clinical Orthodontics article discusses the mewing trend.[4][16]

Mechanical-loading research shows bone adapts to strain, and the masseter enlarges in people who clench, grind or chew heavily.[13] No study measures what forceful tongue pressure does to the adult facial skeleton or masseter.

Users report wider masseters, changes in how their cheeks appear and difficulty resting the teeth together after starting hard mewing.[9] A thread describes a gap between the front teeth after combining palatal expansion, thumb pulling and hard mewing, and Wikipedia lists a gap between upper front teeth as a known side effect of palatal expansion, which uses appliances rather than tongue pressure.[11][14]

The documented harm in the mewing story concerns clinical orthotropics. Wikipedia reports that Mike Mew faced a General Dental Council misconduct hearing over harm to child patients, that The Guardian reported on the tribunal on 14 November 2022, that the BBC reported in April 2023 on a treated boy with seizure-like episodes, and that he was struck from the UK dental register in 2024.[5] John Mew's licence was revoked in 2017 over false advertising and breaching patient confidentiality, after a 2010 reprimand.[15]

No studies found. No clinical study has examined forceful tongue pressure on the palate for facial appearance. The wider topic of mewing and orthotropics has one small twin study of professionally delivered orthotropic treatment and commentary articles, none of which tests hard mewing.[1][4][16]

On looksmax.org, hard mewing is both promoted and disputed. One poster claimed it gave forward growth even after puberty when combined with chin tucks and sprinting, calling it more effective than drugs, while replies asked for photographic evidence.[8] Another thread describes a user who began hard mewing and noticed wider masseters, hollower cheeks and a harder time resting the teeth together, and asked whether an overbite was responsible.[9] A third user lists hard mewing, chewing, thumb pulling, belt pulling, bonesmashing and chin tucking as parts of a daily regimen.[10] A further thread asks what to do about a gap between the front teeth after palate expansion, thumb pulling and hard mewing.[11]

The discussion shows the belief that more force means more effect, and an opposing view in other threads that it is unproven or counterproductive; one thread title urges members to stop hard mewing.[12] Mewing broadly also entered mainstream media as a meme, with The Independent reporting in March 2024 on students mewing in class.[5]

timeline.event: John Mew, founder of orthotropics, is born in Royal Tunbridge Wells.[15]
Mew proposes the "Tropic Premise" of malocclusion as a postural condition.[15]

The Guardian reports on the Mike Mew misconduct tribunal (14 November).[5]
Mike Mew is struck from the UK dental register.[5]
John Mew dies on 25 June, aged 96.[15]

lore.intro: Hard mewing appears on looksmax.org as the intensive version of mewing, usually in routines with other bone-related practices, with both enthusiasts and sceptics posting threads.[6][10][12]

claims.claim: Hard mewing causes forward growth even after puberty
claims.believers: A poster says it gave substantial forward growth after puberty when combined with chin tucks and sprinting, and others report multi-year routines.[8][26]
claims.experts: No published studies have examined it; the AAO says there is no evidence that mewing improves the jaw.[5]

claims.claim: Hard mewing widens the jaw or enlarges the masseters
claims.believers: A user reports that masseters became wider after starting hard mewing, which he regards as a mixed result.[9]
claims.experts: Masseter enlargement is documented in people who clench or grind their teeth or chew constantly, but no study links it to tongue pressure.[13]

claims.claim: Hard mewing combined with thumb pulling and expanders produces visible change
claims.believers: Members describe combined regimens, and one asks about a diastema after combining the practices.[10][11]
claims.experts: Palatal expansion is an orthodontic treatment with known side effects including a gap between upper front teeth; it uses appliances, not tongue pressure.[14]

claims.claim: Pressing harder produces more effect than light resting posture
claims.believers: Posters describe force as the difference between ordinary mewing and results.[3][25]
claims.experts: Orthotropic teaching centres on resting posture, and no study compares forceful with light tongue pressure.[15][5]

claims.claim: Hard mewing fixes head and neck posture
claims.believers: A poster credits hard mewing with chin tucks for neck stability and head position.[8]
claims.experts: Orthotropics links tongue posture and head posture in theory, but the published literature is limited to the 2007 twin study and commentaries.[1][4]

claims.claim: Hard mewing works best during growth
claims.believers: Threads post results from users in their mid-teens.[27]
claims.experts: The twin study treated young patients with professional appliances; no study of self-directed adult practice exists.[1]

claims.claim: Orthodontists reject mewing to protect surgery and braces income
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread title asserts that orthodontists oppose mewing out of self-interest.[28]
claims.experts: The AAO states no evidence mewing improves the jaw, and Wikipedia reports disciplinary findings against the Mews over harm to child patients.[5]

angle.text: People practise hard mewing hoping that firm tongue pressure will move the upper jaw forward and define the jawline over time. Users also report that it enlarges the masseter muscles, which can widen the lower face, and that holding the posture changes how the neck and head sit.[8][9] These effects are reported by users; no clinical study has measured them.
